Alan García (Latin American; 23 May 1949 - 17 April 2019) was a Peruvian politician who served as President of Peru for two non-consecutive terms, from 1985 to 1990 and from 2006 to 2011.

Grand Duchess Tatiana Nikolaevna of Russia
Asenath (Koine) is a minor figure in the Book of Genesis.
A former SAS trooper turned wilderness-TV host, in 2009 he became the Scout Association's youngest-ever Chief Scout at age 35 — who is this British adventurer?
Bear Grylls (born 7 June 1974) is a British adventurer, television presenter and former SAS trooper.

Before founding the party Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam and becoming chief minister of Tamil Nadu in 2026, this man was one of India's highest-paid Tamil cinema stars — making his leading debut in a 1992 film directed by his own father. Who is he?
C. Joseph Vijay (born 22 June 1974) is an Indian politician and former actor who is currently serving as the ninth chief minister of Tamil Nadu since May 2026.
Nicknamed the 'Father-in-law of Europe' for marrying his children into so many royal houses, which Danish king reigned from 1863 to 1906?
Christian IX (8 April 1818 - 29 January 1906) was King of Denmark from 15 November 1863 until his death in 1906.
This American anthropologist and anarchist gave the Occupy movement a leading voice and wrote provocative books like Debt: The First 5,000 Years and Bullshit Jobs — who was he?
David Graeber (February 12, 1961 - September 2, 2020) was an American anthropologist and anarchist social and political activist.
Often called the greatest jurist of the Elizabethan and Jacobean eras, this English barrister rose from the Inner Temple to Speaker of the House of Commons and Attorney General. Who was he?
Edward Coke (CUUK, formerly; 1 February 1552 - 3 September 1634) was an English barrister, judge, and politician.
Ascending to the Iraqi throne at age three after his father's death, this monarch was killed in the 1958 coup that ended the Hashemite monarchy — who is he?
Faisal II (2 May 1935 - 14 July 1958) was the last King of Iraq.

An Egyptian military revolutionary seized power in 1954, introduced sweeping land reforms, and became a hero across the Arab world by nationalizing a crucial waterway. Who led Egypt as its second president for sixteen transformative years?
Gamal Abdel Nasser (15 January 1918 - 28 September 1970) was an Egyptian military officer and revolutionary who served as the second president of Egypt from 1954 until his death in 1970.
This art-collecting Russian general and patron helped install Catherine the Great on the throne before his infidelities cost him his influence — who is he?
Grigory Orlov (17 October 1734 - 24 April 1783) was a Russian general and patron of arts who was Prince of the Holy Roman Empire (1772) and a favourite of Empress Catherine the Great.
House speaker, secretary of state, and a three-time loser of the presidency, this Kentuckian earned the nickname 'the Great Compromiser' for defusing sectional crises — who was he?
Henry Clay (April 12, 1777 - June 29, 1852) was an American lawyer, statesman, and diplomat who represented Kentucky in both the United States House of Representatives and the United States Senate.
Son of a former prime minister, this Cambodian leader rose through the Royal Cambodian Army to deputy commander-in-chief before taking his father's job in 2023 — who is he?

Hun Manet (born 20 October 1977) is a Cambodian politician and military officer who has served as Prime Minister of Cambodia and Vice President of the ruling Cambodian People's Party (CPP) since 2023.
This mid-1740s bid to restore the exiled Stuarts to the British throne began in the Scottish Highlands and ended when its army turned back from Derby in December — which rebellion?
Jacobite rising of 1745 was an attempt to regain the British throne for the exiled House of Stuart.

This German-American newspaper editor and orator popularized 'propaganda of the deed' in the United States and was jailed several times after publishing literature on how to build and use bombs — who was he?
Johann Most (February 5, 1846 - March 17, 1906) was a German-American Social Democratic and then anarchist politician, newspaper editor, and orator.
This Indian politician has served since 2024 as both Minister of Communications and Minister of Development of the North Eastern Region — who is he?
Jyotiraditya Scindia (born 1 January 1971; Hindi) is an Indian politician who is serving as the 43rd Minister of Communications and 10th Minister of Development of North Eastern Region since 2024.

Co-recipient with the United Nations of the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize, this Ghanaian diplomat served as the organization's seventh secretary-general and later chaired an international group founded by Nelson Mandela — who was he?
Kofi Annan (8 April 1938 - 18 August 2018) was a Ghanaian diplomat and statesman who served as the seventh secretary-general of the United Nations from 1997 to 2006.
Once seen as Mao Zedong's likely successor, this Chinese politician served as head of state from 1959 until he was purged during the Cultural Revolution — who was he?
Liu Shaoqi (24 November 1898 - 12 November 1969) was a Chinese revolutionary and politician.
Orphaned of his father at three, this Roman emperor became the last of the Five Good Emperors and is remembered as much for his Stoic philosophy as his reign — who was he?
Marcus Aurelius (26 April 121 - 17 March 180) was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher.
Said to have lived 969 years — the longest recorded lifespan in the Bible — this patriarch was the grandfather of Noah — who is he?
Methuselah was a biblical patriarch and a figure in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
Possibly Arthur's own son in early Welsh tradition, this Arthurian figure was later recast as a treacherous nephew associated with the fateful Battle of Camlann. Who is he?
Mordred (or) is a major figure in the legend of King Arthur.
Born at Tsarskoye Selo and widely thought ill-prepared to rule, this monarch led his empire into World War I before abdicating in 1917 — and in 1918 his whole family was murdered. Who was he?
Nicholas II was Emperor of Russia from 1894 to 1917.
Once Britain's youngest sitting MP, this baronet drifted from the Conservatives to Labour before founding the British Union of Fascists in 1932 — who is it?
Oswald Mosley (16 November 1896 - 3 December 1980), was a British politician who rose to fame during the 1920s and 1930s when, disillusioned with mainstream politics, he turned to fascism.
This longtime CPI(M) state secretary became Kerala's 12th Chief Minister in 2016 and later served as Leader of the Opposition — who is he?
Pinarayi Vijayan (born 24 May 1945) is an Indian politician who served as the 12th Chief Minister of Kerala from 25 May 2016 to 18 May 2026.
Charged with murder after a deadly 1992 standoff with federal agents at his Idaho cabin, this self-proclaimed separatist was ultimately acquitted of most charges — who is he?
Randy Weaver (January 3, 1948 - May 11, 2022) was an American survivalist and self-proclaimed white separatist.
He was the longest-serving commandant of Auschwitz, in charge across two stretches between 1940 and 1945 — what was his name?
Rudolf Höss (also H, Hoe, or Hoess; 25 November 1901 - 16 April 1947) was a German SS officer and the commandant of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
Briefly governor of Moscow Oblast in 2012, this member of Putin's inner circle led Russia's defence ministry until 2024, when he moved to secretary of the Security Council — who is he?
Sergei Shoigu (born 21 May 1955) is a Russian politician and military officer who has served as secretary of the Security Council since 2024.
Gaining wide use in American political discourse of the 1930s and '40s, this doctrine holds that governing authority carries some legitimacy, standing opposed to anarchism — what's it called?
Statism (from French, tat 'state') is the doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree.
Before he became the Supreme Court's first African-American justice, this lawyer won 29 of the 32 civil rights cases he argued there, capped by 1954's Brown v. Board of Education — who is he?
Thurgood Marshall (July 2, 1908 - January 24, 1993) was an American lawyer who served as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States from 1967 until 1991.
Spanning roughly 800 to 1050 CE, this era saw Scandinavian raiders, traders, and settlers push across Europe and reach as far as North America — which age?

Viking Age (about 800-1050 CE) was the period during the Middle Ages when Norsemen known as Vikings undertook large-scale raiding, colonising, conquest, and trading throughout Europe and reached North America.
Starting in his father's grocery business at fifteen, this English industrialist built an empire on Sunlight Soap, Lux, and Lifebuoy. Who was he?
William Lever, 1st Viscount Leverhulme (19 September 1851 - 7 May 1925) was an English industrialist, philanthropist, and politician.

This Soviet partisan was executed by invading Nazi forces after committing acts of sabotage, and was posthumously declared a Hero of the Soviet Union, becoming one of its most revered heroines — who was she?
Zoya Kosmodemyanskaya (September 13, 1923 - November 29, 1941) was a Soviet partisan.
Traditionally chanted by a muezzin from a mosque's minaret before each of the five daily prayers, what is this Islamic call known as?
Adhan: Islamic call to prayer. The five prayer times are known in Arabic as fajr (فجر), dhuhr (ظهر), asr (عصر), maghrib (مغرب), and isha (عشاء).

Alp Arslan: Sultan of the Seljuk Empire from 1063 to 1072.
Arrested in the US in 2010 as part of a Russian espionage ring, this former agent-turned-media personality was later swapped back to Russia in a prisoner exchange — who is she?
Anna Chapman: Russian intelligence agent, media personality and model (born 1982)
A onetime communist who embraced privatization, this physicist-turned-leader ran Kyrgyzstan from 1990 until 2005, when the Tulip Revolution swept him from power. Who was he?

Askar Akayev: President of Kyrgyzstan from 1990 to 2005. Akayev became president of Kyrgyzstan in 1990, a year before the Fall of the Soviet Union, and he remained in his post after Kyrgyzstan became independent.

Drawing on Bolshevism and anarchism, this Indian revolutionary's largely symbolic bombing of the Central Legislative Assembly and a jail hunger strike made him a folk hero — and a martyr after his execution at age 23; who was he?
It began in 1703 as a townhouse for a duke, then George III bought it in 1761 as a private home for Queen Charlotte — today it's a monarch's official London residence. Which building?

Buckingham Palace: Official London residence of the British monarch. Buckingham Palace (UK:) is the official residence and the administrative headquarters of the monarch of the United Kingdom in London.
Derived from the Latin word for 'to assess,' this systematic count of a population's members is recommended by the UN to be conducted at least once every ten years. What is it?
Census: Compilation of information about a given population.
Commemorating the birth of Jesus and observed by billions on 25 December, its liturgical preparation season begins on the first Sunday of what?

Christmas is an annual celebration commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ, observed primarily on December 25. A liturgical feast central to Christianity, its preparation begins on the First Sunday of Advent.

Also called the War of Candia, this 24-year struggle pitted Venice and her allies — the Knights of Malta, the Papacy, France — against the Ottomans, mostly over Venice's richest overseas island. What conflict was it?
Cretan War (1645–1669): Conflict between the Republic of Venice and the Ottoman Empire (1645–1669)

Dean Phillips: American businessman and politician (born 1969)

Doug Burgum: American politician and businessman (born 1956)
Elected to Israel's Knesset at just 28, this politician later served two terms as Mayor of Jerusalem before becoming prime minister from 2006 to 2009 — who is he?
Ehud Olmert: Prime Minister of Israel from 2006 to 2009. The son of a former Herut politician, Olmert was first elected to the Knesset for Likud in 1973, at the age of 28.

This Argentine politician served as the first Chief of Government of Buenos Aires from 1996 to 1999 before becoming president, a role he resigned from in 2001 — who is he?
Fernando de la Rúa: President of Argentina from 1999 to 2001. De la Rúa was born in Córdoba, and entered politics after graduating with a degree in law.

It began with the Estates General of 1789 — the first such meeting since 1614 — and ended a decade later with the Coup of 18 Brumaire, leaving behind ideas now central to liberal democracy. What upheaval is this?
French Revolution: 1789–1799 sociopolitical change in France.
A Royal Navy officer charted the Pacific coast from California up to Alaska so thoroughly that an island, a major city, and a mountain all bear his name — who was he?
George Vancouver: Royal Navy officer and explorer (1757–1798)
Serving as Texas's attorney general before becoming its governor in 2015, this Republican is now the longest-serving incumbent governor in the United States — who is he?

Greg Abbott: Governor of Texas since 2015. Gregory Wayne Abbott ( ABB-ət; born November 13, 1957) is an American politician, attorney, and jurist who has served since 2015 as the 48th governor of Texas.
As a boy he pledged to his father to 'never be a friend of Rome,' then as a Carthaginian general sparked the Second Punic War by attacking Saguntum in 218 BC — who is he?
Hannibal: Carthaginian general and statesman (247–183/181 BC)

Heir to his older brother's title, he became England's king at 17 and transformed the English church's relationship with Rome—losing multiple heirs in the process as he pursued his dynastic ambitions. Which Tudor king forever changed religious and political history?
Henry VIII: King of England from 1509 to 1547.

This European noble dynasty's founder led the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule, and a later prince orchestrated England's Glorious Revolution — which royal family currently reigns over the Netherlands?
House of Orange-Nassau: European dynasty. Several members of the house served during the Eighty Years' War and after as stadtholder ("governor"; Dutch: stadhouder) during the Dutch Republic.

Nicknamed the 'Flying Tank' by Soviet ground troops, this WWII ground-attack aircraft became, together with its successor, the most-produced military plane design in aviation history — which aircraft?
De Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter

Ilyushin Il-2: Soviet ground attack aircraft of WWII. The Ilyushin Il-2 (Russian: Илью́шин Ил-2) is a ground-attack plane that was produced by the Soviet Union in large numbers during the Second World War.

Nicknamed "Boney," this British general helped plan the tank attack at Cambrai and dreamed up a fully mechanised "Plan 1919" — making this fascist, occultist theorist one of the progenitors of blitzkrieg. Who was he?
J. F. C. Fuller: British Army general (1878–1966)
A former Salesian priest who preached liberation theology, he served multiple stints as president of Haiti — twice driven into exile, in 1991 and again in 2004. Who is he?
Jean-Bertrand Aristide: Former president of Haiti (born 1953)

This British naval officer led Arctic expeditions and governed Van Diemen's Land before his final 1845 attempt at the Northwest Passage left his ships icebound off King William Island, where he died. Who was he?
John Franklin: British naval officer and explorer (1786–1847)
Nicknamed the "Restorer of the Laws," this wealthy landowner turned his ranch workers into a private army and ruled Buenos Aires Province as a caudillo — who was he?
Juan Manuel de Rosas: Argentine politician and general (1793–1877)
He left school at 12 to work the family farm yet rose to become both prime minister and, uniquely in his country's history, also governor-general of New Zealand — who was he?
The first chancellor of West Germany and a founding father of the European Union, this former mayor of Cologne led his country's postwar recovery from 1949 to 1963 — who was he?
Konrad Adenauer: Chancellor of West Germany from 1949 to 1963. Adenauer belied his age by his intense work habits and his uncanny political instinct.
Born to a working-class family in Kamenskoye, he led the USSR as General Secretary from 1964 until his death — a tenure second in length only to Stalin's. Who was he?
Leonid Brezhnev: Leader of the Soviet Union from 1964 to 1982.
Married to Eleanor of Aquitaine, this 12th-century monarch's union briefly extended his Capetian lands to the Pyrenees before the couple's marriage soured during the Second Crusade — who is he?
Louis VII of France: King of the Franks from 1137 to 1180.
The niece of Japan's current emperor, this art historian gave up her imperial title in 2021 upon marrying a commoner, as required by law — who is she?
A general under Julius Caesar in Gaul, this Roman was left to administer Italy while Caesar hunted his rivals abroad — then teamed with Lepidus and Octavian after the assassination. Who is he?
Mark Antony: Roman politician and general (83–30 BC)
Ascending the Ottoman throne at age six in 1648 after his father's overthrow, this sultan reigned longer than all but Suleiman the Magnificent and was nicknamed 'the Hunter' — who is he?
Mehmed IV: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1648 to 1687.
Equated by the Romans with the Greek goddess Athena, this member of the Capitoline Triad favors an owl as her sacred creature — who is she?

A former physics teacher turned politician, this four-term Turkish MP ran as the main opposition's presidential candidate in 2018, finishing second to the incumbent with just over 30% of the vote — who is he?
Muharrem İnce: Turkish politician. Muharrem İnce (Turkish: [inˈdʒe]; born 4 May 1964) is a Turkish physics teacher, school principal, sport executive, and politician.
Serving as the 41st U.S. vice president under Gerald Ford, this wealthy New York governor previously held posts under three earlier presidents dating back to the 1940s — who is he?
Nelson Rockefeller: Vice President of the United States from 1974 to 1977.
Founded in 1961 to spur economic progress and world trade, this 38-member intergovernmental forum unites high-income, advanced economies committed to democracy and the market economy. What is it?
OECD: Intergovernmental economic organisation. OECD members are highly developed countries with advanced economies typically considered efficient and high-income.

First championed at an 1900 conference organized by a Trinidadian barrister to protest colonial land theft, this movement seeks unity among indigenous peoples and diaspora descendants of one continent — which movement?
Pan-Africanism: Movement encouraging solidarity among people of African ancestry.

An oligarch who once headed Ukraine's National Bank council, he won the presidency in a 2014 landslide with over 55% in the first round and led the country through the early war in Donbas — who is he?
Petro Poroshenko: President of Ukraine from 2014 to 2019.

Born at Windsor Castle with her grandmother, the queen, in attendance, this granddaughter of a British monarch married her father's cousin, a Royal Navy officer, and later became Marchioness of Milford Haven — who was she?

A top West Point graduate and U.S. Army engineer for 32 years, he switched sides to command the Army of Northern Virginia until its 1865 surrender, earning fame as one of the war's craftiest tacticians. Which Confederate general is it?
Robert E. Lee: Confederate States Army general (1807–1870)
The seventh adult man ever to embrace Islam, this military commander led the conquest of a Sasanian capital and founded the garrison city of Kufa — who is he?
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: Muslim general (c. 595 – 674)

His 1971 book "Rules for Radicals: A Pragmatic Primer" defended both confrontation and compromise, drawn from his work with Chicago's Industrial Areas Foundation organizing poor communities — which American activist wrote it?
Saul Alinsky: American activist and political theorist (1909–1972)
Known by the kunya Abu Idris, this Chechen guerrilla commander helped recapture Grozny in 1996 and later masterminded some of Russia's worst hostage-taking attacks — who is he?
Stepping up from hostess for her assassinated husband, this Sri Lankan politician became, in 1960, the first woman in the world elected prime minister — who was she?
Sirimavo Bandaranaike: Prime Minister of Sri Lanka (1916–2000)
Released from Dutch detention by invading Japanese forces in WWII, this nationalist leader went on to become the very first president of his newly independent nation. Who is he?
Sukarno: President of Indonesia from 1945 to 1967.
This brief conflict ran from June 27 to July 7, 1991, ending when the Brioni Accords settled Slovenia's break from Yugoslavia — what was it called?

Ten-Day War: 1991 Slovenia-Yugoslavia conflict. It was fought between the Slovenian Territorial Defence and the Slovenian National Police Force on one side, and the Yugoslav People's Army on the other.
Operated by the White Star Line, this British ocean liner struck an iceberg on her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York and sank in the early hours of 15 April 1912. Name the ship.
RMS Titanic, operated by the White Star Line, sank in the early hours of 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg on her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City.

Formed after the Napoleonic Wars by fusing the old Dutch Republic, the Austrian-ruled Low Countries, and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège into a buffer state under William I of Orange-Nassau, this polity collapsed with the 1830 Belgian Revolution — what was it called?
United Kingdom of the Netherlands: European territory (1815–1839)
Held hostage by the Ottomans as a boy, this three-time Voivode of Wallachia is honored as a Christian hero in Romania for fighting the empire. Who is he?
Vlad the Impaler: 15th-century ruler of Wallachia.
Canada's first French-Canadian prime minister, he served 15 unbroken years from 1896 and built his legacy on compromise between English and French Canada — who is he?
Wilfrid Laurier: Prime Minister of Canada from 1896 to 1911. Sir Henri Charles Wilfrid Laurier (November 20, 1841 – February 17, 1919) was the seventh prime minister of Canada from 1896 to 1911.
Known by his initials, this Indian politician served as chief minister of Andhra Pradesh for two terms before dying in a 2009 helicopter crash over a forest — who was he?

COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Who among these is a physicist?
Louis Slotin is a physicist. Louis Alexander Slotin ( SLOHT-in; 1 December 1910 – 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
Pick the chemist from these four.
James Lovelock is a chemist. James Ephraim Lovelock (26 July 1919 – 26 July 2022) was an English independent scientist, environmentalist and futurist.
What is the atomic number of Unbiunium?
Unbiunium, also known as eka-actinium or element 121, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubu and atomic number 121.
In what year was J. Robert Oppenheimer born?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: In 1941, Oppenheimer was briefed about nuclear weapon design by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant.
In what year did Archimedes die?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
In what year was Iron discovered?
Iron is a chemical element; it has symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum 'iron') and atomic number 26.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Which country is Sukhoi Su-57 from?
Sukhoi Su-57: Russia. The Sukhoi Su-57 (Russian: Сухой Су-57; NATO reporting name: Felon) is a twin-engine stealth multirole fighter aircraft developed by Sukhoi.
Who is credited with discovering Gaussian integral?
Gaussian integral: Leonhard Euler. The integral has a wide range of applications.
Who is credited with discovering Aspirin?
Aspirin: Raffaele Piria. Aspirin is used to treat inflammatory conditions including Kawasaki disease, pericarditis, and rheumatic fever.
Who is credited with discovering Boron?
Boron: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.

The active component of vinegar and the second simplest carboxylic acid, this colourless liquid with the formula CH₃COOH has been produced in large quantities since the third millennium BCE. What is this acid?
Acetic acid is an acidic, colourless liquid and organic compound with the chemical formula CH3COOH (also written as CH3CO2H, C2H4O2, or HC2H3O2).
A military pilot who became the first astronaut representing Turkey, he reached the International Space Station on 18 January 2024 aboard the Axiom Mission 3 flight — who is he?
Alper Gezeravcı (born 2 December 1979) is a military pilot and the first Turkish astronaut.
What term describes the discipline of measuring human body dimensions, applied everywhere from ergonomics and architecture to tracking historical living standards?
Anthropometry (from Ancient Greek (nthrpos) 'human' and (mtron) 'measure') refers to the measurement of the human individual.

Distinguished from celestial mechanics by asking what heavenly bodies ARE rather than where they are, this science applies physics and chemistry to the Sun, stars, galaxies, and exoplanets — which discipline?
Astrophysics is a science that applies the methods and principles of physics and chemistry in the study of astronomical objects and phenomena including the universe.
This steroid medication treats conditions ranging from rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis to asthma, and is also given before preterm birth to help speed a baby's lung development — what drug is it?
Betamethasone is a steroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin, typically in cream, lotion, or liquid forms.

Derived from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart', this medical term describes a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes a red flag, sometimes just a sign of a well-conditioned athlete. Name the condition?
Bradycardia (brads), meaning "slow", and (karda), meaning "heart", also called bradyarrhythmia, is a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute (BPM).
Caused by an overgrowth of a common yeast, this fungal infection is known as thrush when it affects the mouth and can also cause a genital yeast infection — name the condition?
Candidiasis is a fungal infection due to any species of yeasts in the genus Candida or those that were formerly classified in genus Candida but are now classified in the genus Candidozyma.
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like plant is a staple in calming herbal tea, beer brewing, and even garden ground cover — what is it?
Chamomile (American English) or camomile (British English; see spelling differences) (or) is the common name for several daisy-like plants of the family Asteraceae.
Born near Toulouse, this French inventor is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer — though in 1870 he was also an early enthusiast of cycling in France; who was he?
Clément Ader (French; 2 April 1841 - 3 May 1925) was a French inventor and engineer who was born near Toulouse in Muret, Haute-Garonne, and died in Toulouse.
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on the region, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Western Hemisphere — what is it?
Cougar (Puma concolor), also called puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther, is a large feline native to the Americas.
Caused by either too little insulin or cells that ignore it, this condition keeps blood sugar stubbornly high and comes chiefly in a type 1 and a type 2 — what is it?
Diabetes is a group of common endocrine diseases characterized by sustained high blood sugar levels.
This social science examines the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services, analyzing everything from individual agents to entire economies. What discipline is this?
Economics is a social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services.
This class of mental health condition is defined by an enduring, pervasive pattern of behavior, emotion, and thought that deviates from social norms and develops early in life. What is it?
Erythritol is an organic compound, the naturally occurring achiral meso four-carbon sugar alcohol (or polyol).
Which evergreen conifer genus has needle-like leaves attached singly to the branch by a circular base, and cones that stand upright like a cedar's rather than hanging down? What is it?
Fir are evergreen coniferous trees belonging to the genus Abies in the family Pinaceae.
Native to Pacific coastal waters from Alaska to Baja California, this giant burrowing clam can grow a siphon over three feet long and live for more than a century — which creature?
Geoduck (Panopea generosa) is a species of very large saltwater clam in the family Hiatellidae.

These common coastal seabirds, most closely related to terns and skimmers, were once known by an older name still surviving in some English dialects and cognate with the German word Möwe — what birds are they?
Gull (see Taxonomy), are seabirds of the subfamily Larinae.
First identified in 1910, this organic compound is stored in mast cells and basophils and, though not made by classic endocrine glands, still acts as a local hormone — what compound is it?
Histamine is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.

This American scientist co-authored a landmark 1953 paper with Francis Crick proposing the double-helix structure of DNA, building on research by Rosalind Franklin, and shared a 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery — who is he?
James Watson (April 6, 1928 - November 6, 2025) was an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist.

Sharing the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, this ethologist was among the first to decode the honey bee's waggle dance — a theory greeted with such skepticism that it took decades to be vindicated. Who was he?
Karl von Frisch (20 November 1886 - 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.

This Hungarian-born physicist conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, drafted the famous letter Einstein signed to launch the Manhattan Project, then later petitioned President Truman not to drop the bomb on civilians — who was he?

Leo Szilard (born Le Spitz; February 11, 1898 - May 30, 1964) was a Hungarian-born American physicist, biologist and inventor who made numerous important discoveries in nuclear physics and the biological sciences.
Reclassified in 2021 as part of the order Psocodea alongside booklice and barklice, these tiny wingless parasites cement their eggs to a single host for life — what are they called?
Louse (pl.: lice) is the common name for any member of the infraorder Phthiraptera, which contains nearly 5,000 species of wingless parasitic insects.
Google's employee No. 20 and its first woman software engineer, she later left to run a famous internet company as CEO from 2012 until Verizon bought it — who is she?
Marissa Mayer (born May 30, 1975) is an American business executive, software engineer, and investor who served as president and chief executive officer of Yahoo!
What neurological disorder causes moderate-to-severe, often one-sided headaches, frequently accompanied by nausea, light and sound sensitivity, and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura'?
Migraine is a neurological disorder that causes moderate-to-severe headaches. The pain usually affects one side of the head.
With somewhere between 66 and 70 species across nine subfamilies, this carnivore family stretches from tiny weasels all the way up to the wolverine. What is it?
Mustelidae (from Latin mustela, weasel) are a diverse family of carnivoran mammals, including weasels, badgers, otters, sea otters, polecats, martens, grisons and wolverines.

Considered primary if a child has never had a long dry stretch, this common childhood condition — usually a developmental delay rather than an illness — is commonly called bedwetting. What's its clinical name?
Nocturnal enuresis (NE), also informally called bedwetting, is involuntary urination while asleep after the age at which bladder control usually begins.
Derived from an ancient Roman unit called the uncia, this unit of mass equals 1/16 of a pound in its common form, though a heavier 'troy' version weighs precious metals — name the unit?
Ounce is any of several different units of mass, weight, or volume and is derived almost unchanged from the uncia, an Ancient Roman unit of measurement.

This short-acting barbiturate is used as a sedative and anticonvulsant in low doses, but in high doses causes fatal respiratory arrest, making it a drug of choice for both veterinary euthanasia and U.S. executions — what is it?
Pentobarbital (US) or pentobarbitone (British and Australian) is a short-acting barbiturate typically used as a sedative, a preanesthetic, and to control convulsions in emergencies.
Native to Eurasia and identifiable by short, blue-green needles, this member of the pine family goes by several regional common names — name the species (Latin binomial)?
Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Split into the strepsirrhines — lemurs and lorisids — and the haplorhines — tarsiers, monkeys and apes — this order ranges in size down to tiny Madame Berthe's — what is it?

Primate is an order of mammals, which is further divided into the strepsirrhines, which include lemurs, galagos, and lorisids; and the haplorhines, which include tarsiers and simians (monkeys and apes).

Founding an organization promoting swadeshi economics against globalization, this Indian social activist later allied with a yoga guru to combine that economic message with the promotion of yoga and Ayurveda — who is he?
Rajiv Dixit (30 November 1967 - 30 November 2010) was an Indian social activist who founded the Azadi Bachao Andolan.

This English X-ray crystallographer's photographs were crucial to unraveling the structure of DNA, yet her contribution went largely unrecognized in her lifetime, earning her posthumous nicknames like "the wronged heroine" — who was she?
Rosalind Franklin (25 July 1920 - 16 April 1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer.
With segmented bony armor, an upright posture, and a curling prehensile tail, these 46 species of tiny bony fish are cousins to the pipefishes and seadragons — what are they?
Seahorse (also written sea-horse and sea horse) is any of 46 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus.
Once placed alone in the genus Uncia before phylogenetics moved it into Panthera, this high-altitude cat ranges across the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas — what is it?
Snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is a species of large cat in the genus Panthera of the family Felidae.
Lacking the powder down that herons and ibises use to clean off fish slime, these bill-clattering wading birds come in 20 living species across six genera — which birds?
Stork are large, long-legged, long-necked wading birds with long, stout bills.

Equal to one weber per square metre, this SI unit of magnetic flux density was adopted in 1960 and named for a Serbian-American electrical engineer, on the proposal of a Slovenian engineer — name this unit?
Tesla (unit) (symbol: T) is the unit of magnetic flux density (B) (also called magnetic B-field) in the International System of Units (SI).
Roughly eight times more potent than an older analogue, this bleeding-control medication is also prescribed for hereditary angioedema — what is it?
Tranexamic acid is a medication used to treat or prevent excessive blood loss from major trauma, postpartum bleeding, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds, and heavy menstruation.
This British-American structural biologist shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for revealing the ribosome's structure and later led the Royal Society as president — who is he?
Venki Ramakrishnan (born 1952) is a British-American structural biologist.
Marketed under names like Rompun, this veterinary sedative and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist is often combined with ketamine for animal anesthesia and used as an emetic in cats — what is it?

Xylazine is a structural analog of clonidine and an 2-adrenergic receptor agonist, sold under many trade names worldwide, most notably the Bayer brand name Rompun, as well as Anased, Sedazine and Chanazine.
Known by the common name yarrow, this pungent, fernleaved plant in the daisy family is used in traditional medicine and as livestock feed — what is its scientific name?
Achillea millefolium: Species of plant. Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
A former IMF economist, this politician has served as President of Ivory Coast since 2010 after earlier stints as the country's prime minister in the early 1990s — who is he?
Alassane Ouattara: President of Ivory Coast since 2010. Ouattara became the president of the Rally of the Republicans (RDR), an Ivorian political party, in 1999.
Also known as shadbush, serviceberry, or juneberry, this rose-family shrub's berries inspired the name of a Canadian city — which genus?
First described by a German entomologist in 1818 and known as the 'marsh mosquito,' this genus is the only one that transmits malaria to humans — which genus is it?
Anopheles: Genus of mosquito. The genus Anopheles diverged from other mosquitoes approximately 100 million years ago (mya), and, like other mosquitoes, the eggs, larvae, and pupae are aquatic.
The third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere at nearly 1%, this noble gas takes its name from an Ancient Greek word meaning 'lazy' or 'inactive' — what element is it?
Argon: Chemical element with atomic number 18 (Ar)
From the Greek for "self-devouring," this lysosome-driven process lets a cell tidily break down and recycle its own worn-out parts — what is it?
Autophagy: Process of cells digesting parts of themselves.
Spurred by the 1980 failure of Operation Eagle Claw, this American tiltrotor blends a helicopter's vertical takeoff with a turboprop's long-range cruise — what aircraft is it?
Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey: Military transport tiltrotor.
This insect order unites cockroaches with termites, after genetic evidence showed termites are actually evolved, eusocial cockroaches. What's the order called?
Blattodea: Order of insects that includes cockroaches and termites.
Created in 1993 by Swiss student Urban Müller, this esoteric programming language uses just eight simple commands and is often cited as a 'Turing tarpit' — what is it called?
Brainfuck: Esoteric, minimalist programming language. While Brainfuck is fully Turing-complete, it is not intended for practical use but to challenge and amuse programmers.
Discovered in 1817 simultaneously by two German chemists as an impurity in zinc carbonate, this soft silvery-white metal shares chemical traits with zinc and mercury — which element?
Cadmium: Chemical element with atomic number 48 (Cd)

A German child prodigy turned director of the Göttingen Observatory, this mathematician, astronomer, and physicist made landmark contributions across number theory, algebra, statistics, and probability — who is he?
Carl Friedrich Gauss: German polymath and scholar (1777–1855)
Documented anatomically since the time of Hippocrates over 2,000 years ago, this roughly 4-centimeter-long fibromuscular organ connects the vagina to the uterine cavity. What structure is this?
Cervix: Lower part of the uterus in the female reproductive system.
This Dutch scientist discovered Saturn's largest moon and invented the pendulum clock, the most accurate timekeeper for nearly three centuries — who is he?
Christiaan Huygens: Dutch mathematician and physicist (1629–1695)
Thought extinct since the age of dinosaurs 66 million years ago, this lobe-finned fish was found alive off the west Indian Ocean, more closely related to lungfish than typical fish — what is it?
Also known as the Cornelian cherry, this dogwood-family shrub or small tree is native to western and southern Europe as well as southwestern Asia — what's its scientific name?
Cornus mas: Species of flowering plant in the family Cornaceae.
This closed sac in the body, distinct from an abscess of pus, forms a shell of abnormal cells and may contain air, fluid, or semi-solid material — what is it, medically?
Cyst: Closed sac growth on the body. A cyst is a closed sac in the body, having a distinct envelope and division compared with the nearby tissue.

Found in many cough and cold medicines, this morphinan-class compound was approved by the FDA in 2022 as part of a rapid-acting antidepressant combo, but can act as a dissociative hallucinogen at high doses. What substance is it?
Dextromethorphan: Cough suppressant and dissociative drug.
Sold over the counter as Unisom and combined with vitamin B6 to ease morning sickness, this first-generation antihistamine is one of the world's most widely used sleep aids — which drug?
Doxylamine: First-generation antihistamine used as a short-term sedative and hypnotic (sleep aid)
Appointed to the Supreme Court by Barack Obama in 2010, this former Harvard Law dean became the fourth woman ever to serve as a justice — who is she?
Elena Kagan: US Supreme Court justice since 2010.
A rod-shaped gut bacterium that's mostly harmless or even helpful — some strains produce vitamin K2 and fend off nastier microbes — what is its name?
Sold in Italian restaurants as branzino, this slow-growing ocean fish is the most important species farmed commercially in the Mediterranean — what fish is it?
European seabass: Species of fish. It is one of only six species in its family, Moronidae, collectively called the temperate basses.
This beetle family produces light mainly at twilight to attract mates — though some females mimic another species' flash pattern just to lure and eat the males — what are they commonly called?
Firefly: Family of beetles. The Lampyridae are a family of elateroid beetles with more than 2,400 described species, many of which are light-emitting.
Only chefs with three-plus years of rigorous training may legally prepare this potentially lethal Japanese pufferfish dish, whose poison is tetrodotoxin — what is it?
Recognized as the world's longest ray-finned fish, this ribbon-shaped, silvery-blue deep-sea creature is often blamed for sea-serpent legends — which fish?
Giant oarfish: Species of oceanic ray-finned fish.
One of China's 'Four Great Domestic Fish,' this herbivorous freshwater species was later introduced to Europe and the US to control aquatic weeds — which fish?
Grass carp: Species of fish. This Asian carp is the only species of the genus Ctenopharyngodon.

This prehensile, multi-fingered body part sits at the end of primates' forelimbs — koalas famously have two opposable thumbs on each one, while raccoons are often said to have them despite lacking true opposable thumbs. What is it?
Hand: Extremity at the end of an arm or forelimb.

First synthesized in 1940 by chemist Roger Adams via hydrogenation of THC isomers, this psychoactive cannabis-derived compound is sold in vaporizers despite never being drug-approved — which compound?
Also known as dihydrocodeinone, this semi-synthetic opioid is often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain and is sold alone as an extended-release drug called Zohydro ER — what is it?
Hydrocodone: Opioid drug used in pain relief.
This contagious bacterial skin infection — usually from Staph or Strep — most often shows up as yellowish crusts on the face, arms or legs. What's it called?
A Harvard chemistry professor who studied chlorophyll and helped develop poison gas in WWI, he later became Harvard's president and the first U.S. ambassador to West Germany — who is he?
Nicknamed "Marvellous Merchiston," this 16th-century Scottish laird discovered logarithms and popularized the decimal point — who was this mathematical wizard?
Deafened by childhood illness and rerouted from competitive diving, she became a Hollywood stunt pioneer and earned the title 'the fastest woman in the world.' Who was she?
Kitty O'Neil: American stuntwoman and racer (1946–2018)
Named after the Latin for 'ghosts of the dead' for their large eyes and nocturnal habits, these primates are found only on Madagascar — what are they?
Lemur: Clade of primates endemic to the island of Madagascar.
This four-engine American turboprop can land on dirt strips and unprepared runways, then moonlight as a gunship, a flying firefighter, or a weather scout — which versatile workhorse is it?
Lockheed C-130 Hercules: American military transport aircraft.
Nicknamed for a Native American tribe, this mulberry-family tree produces a bumpy, orange-like fruit that oozes sticky white latex and is rarely eaten by animals — what's its scientific name?
Maclura pomifera: Plant species in the fig family.
This American psychologist completed every requirement for a Harvard Ph.D. in 1895 but was denied the degree because of her gender — who was she?
Mary Whiton Calkins: American philosopher and psychologist. In 1903, Calkins was the twelfth in a listing of fifty psychologists with the most merit, chosen by her peers.

From a Greek word meaning 'change,' this term covers the enzyme-driven reactions that turn food into usable energy and building blocks while excreting waste — letting organisms grow and reproduce. What is it?
Metabolism: Set of chemical reactions in organisms.

Prized for their fur and related to weasels and otters, these semiaquatic carnivores have established wild populations in Britain and Denmark after farm escapes and animal-rights releases — what are they?
Mink: Mammal in the family Mustelidae.
In this autoimmune disease the immune system attacks myelin, the insulation around nerve cells, so the central nervous system can't transmit signals properly — what condition?
Multiple sclerosis: Disease that damages the myelin sheaths around nerves.
Also called roundworms, these mostly free-living animals have a tubular digestive tract with openings at both ends and are grouped with arthropods in the clade Ecdysozoa — what are they?

Introduced in 2001 and originally developed under the name Tier II+, which remotely piloted, high-altitude surveillance aircraft supports the US Air Force with long-endurance radar and infrared sensors?
Northrop Grumman RQ-4 Global Hawk: Unmanned surveillance aircraft. It was initially designed by Ryan Aeronautical (now part of Northrop Grumman), and known as Tier II+ during development.
First domesticated in China's Yangtze River basin more than 8,000 years ago, this grass species is the world's most widely cultivated rice — which species?
Oryza sativa: Species of plant. Oryza sativa belongs to the genus Oryza and the BOP clade in the grass family Poaceae.
Defined as the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends an angle of one arcsecond, this unit equals about 3.26 light-years — which unit?
Parsec: Unit of length in astronomy.
Smaller than 3 millimetres and caused by leaking capillaries, these tiny red or purple skin spots can be forensically significant when found around the eyes or neck — what are they called?
Petechia: Small red or purple blemish on the skin, eyes, etc. due to rupture of capillaries.

Cultivated for its edible nuts since prehistoric times and native to the Mediterranean and the Levant, this pine species has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit — which species?
Pinus pinea: Species of pine tree. Pinus pinea, the Italian stone pine or Mediterranean stone pine, is a tree from the pine family, Pinaceae.
Stockpiled for radiation emergencies, this oral compound floods and shields the thyroid gland — and also treats hyperthyroidism and the skin infection sporotrichosis. Which compound is it?

Harvested from Plantago seeds mainly grown in northern India, this dietary fiber relieves both constipation and mild diarrhea, and can modestly lower cholesterol and blood pressure with regular use. What is it?
Psyllium: Plant used as a dietary fiber.
Named for the noise-making segments at the end of its tail, this venomous pit viper is the leading cause of snakebite injuries in North America. What is it?

This atypical antipsychotic treats schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and autism-related aggression, but carries a risk of the potentially permanent movement disorder tardive dyskinesia — name the drug?
Risperidone: Antipsychotic medication. It is taken either by mouth or by injection (i.e., subcutaneous or intramuscular).
Native to the North Atlantic and North Pacific, these anadromous fish hatch in freshwater gravel beds, mature in the ocean, then return to their birth river to spawn — what are they?
With an eagle-like body perched on crane-like legs and a bare red-orange face, which African bird of prey spends most of its time hunting on foot across the savanna?
Secretarybird: Bird of prey. The secretarybird or secretary bird (Sagittarius serpentarius) is a large bird of prey that is endemic to Africa.
In this rare congenital condition affecting about 1 in 10,000 people, the heart and other major organs sit as a mirror image of their normal position — what's it called?
Situs inversus: Condition in which organs are reversed.

Made of a segmented series of bones cushioned by intervertebral discs, this defining feature of some 50,000 animal species surrounds and protects the nerve tissue running through it — what is it, also known as the backbone?
Spinal column: Bony structure found in vertebrates.
Signified by the minus sign, this arithmetic operation represents removing objects from a collection and is the inverse of addition — which operation is it?
Subtraction: One of the four basic arithmetic operations.
This genus of flowering plants, commonly called dandelions, thrives nearly worldwide in yards, gardens, and roadsides — which genus?
Taraxacum: Genus of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.
Best known for his 1651 work 'Leviathan' and its influential take on social contract theory, this English philosopher once met Galileo while tutoring the Cavendish family across Europe — who was he?
Thomas Hobbes: English philosopher and political theorist (1588–1679)
Only about 76 to 90 nucleotides long, this adaptor molecule reads each three-letter mRNA codon with a matching anticodon and ferries the right amino acid to the ribosome — what is it?
Transfer RNA: RNA that facilitates the addition of amino acids to a new protein.
Element 121, this not-yet-synthesized superactinide is expected to open a brand-new g-block of the periodic table and may sit on the 'island of stability' — what's its placeholder name?
Unbiunium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 121 (Ubu)
Named by a naturalist in 1821, this family of feliform mammals split into genets, civets, and palm civets, and spans Africa to Southeast Asia — what is it?
Viverridae: Family of carnivorans. Viverridae is a family of small to medium-sized feliform mammals, comprising 14 genera with 33 species.
Nominated by Einstein, this Austrian physicist won the 1945 Nobel Prize for describing the exclusion principle and, in 1930, proposed the tiny neutral particle later named the neutrino — who is he?
The symbol for niobium is Nb. Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb and atomic number 41.
The symbol for holmium is Ho. Holmium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ho and atomic number 67.

Jennifer Connelly: Jennifer Lynn Connelly (born December 12, 1970) is an American actress.
In what year was Phil Collins born?
Phil Collins: Philip David Charles Collins (born 30 January 1951) is an English singer, drummer, songwriter, record producer, and actor.
In what year was Matthew Perry born?
Matthew Perry: Matthew Langford Perry (August 19, 1969 – October 28, 2023) was an American and Canadian actor.
In what year was Margot Robbie born?
Margot Robbie: Margot Elise Robbie ( MAR-goh ROB-ee; born 2 July 1990) is an Australian actress and producer.

Paul Mescal: Paul Colm Michael Mescal ( MESS-kəl; born 2 February 1996) is an Irish actor.
